planting.note: Plant tubers 4-5 inches deep in cool, humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade once the soil has warmed in spring; give this Himalayan species a sheltered site and a thick winter mulch, since it is more cold-sensitive than the common North American jack-in-the-pulpit.

directions: Plant tubers 4-5 inches deep in cool, humus-rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring after the soil has warmed; this high-elevation Himalayan species is unusual in the genus for producing just two enormous, broad leaflets per leaf rather than the typical three or more. In late spring the huge, deeply hooded spathe unfurls in mottled maroon-purple and green with a network of pale veining, drawn out into an extraordinarily long, trailing, whip-like tail that can stretch several feet across the ground. It is among the most dramatic and sought-after Arisaema for a shaded collector's bed, best given a sheltered site with a thick winter mulch and excellent drainage to prevent tuber rot. As with all Arisaema, the tuber, foliage, and berries contain irritating calcium oxalate crystals and are toxic if ingested, so keep away from pets and children.

planting.note: Plant tubers 4-5 inches deep in rich, moist, well-drained woodland soil in partial to full shade in mid-spring, in a site sheltered from late frost and strong wind while the tall false stem and flower emerge.

directions: Plant tubers 4-5 inches deep in rich, moist, well-drained woodland soil in partial to full shade in mid-spring; Arisaema speciosum is a Himalayan aroid grown for its dramatically striped, purple-black-and-green hooded spathe, drawn into one of the longest whip-like tails in the genus, often trailing two feet or more from the tip of the hood. The three glossy leaflets, each edged with a fine white line along the central vein, unfurl on a tall, mottled false stem beneath the flower. It prefers a humid, sheltered woodland setting protected from late frost and strong wind, going dormant by late summer once the tuber has stored enough energy for the following year. All parts of the plant contain calcium oxalate crystals and are toxic and irritating if chewed or eaten, so site it away from curious pets or children despite its striking ornamental berries.

planting.note: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in early spring; this Chinese species is one of the more reliable and easy-to-grow Arisaema for a woodland collector's bed.

directions: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in early spring; this Chinese woodland aroid produces a slender, elegant, green-and-white striped hooded spathe named for the fine, hair-like cilia fringing the opening of the hood, drawn out into a slim tail above three broad, glossy leaflets. It is a relatively easy and reliable Arisaema for the woodland garden, multiplying gradually by offsets under consistently moist, humus-rich conditions similar to its Chinese relatives Arisaema consanguineum and Arisaema fargesii. Like other jack-in-the-pulpit relatives, the tuber and berries contain irritating calcium oxalate crystals and are toxic if eaten, so keep the attractive fall fruit away from pets and children.

planting.note: Plant tubers 4-5 inches deep in cool, moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; give it excellent winter drainage and a sheltered spot, since the compact flower sits close to the ground beneath the foliage.

directions: Plant tubers 4-5 inches deep in cool, moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; this Himalayan species takes its name from the prominent, deeply impressed, rib-like veins running the length of its three broad leaflets, which are further marked with a reddish central rib. The dark purple-black hooded spathe, striped with white, appears at or just below the level of the foliage in late spring, giving the plant a lower, more compact profile in bloom than many taller Arisaema relatives. It performs best in a sheltered woodland spot with reliable summer moisture and excellent drainage over winter, going fully dormant by late summer. All parts contain irritating calcium oxalate crystals and are toxic if ingested, so keep it out of reach of pets and children despite its ornamental red berry clusters.

planting.note: Plant tubers 4-6 inches deep in moist, rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in a sheltered spot in spring; this mid-elevation Himalayan species is less cold-hardy than high-alpine Arisaema relatives and appreciates a heavy winter mulch outside its comfortable range.

directions: Plant tubers 4-6 inches deep in moist, rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in a sheltered spot in spring; Arisaema nepenthoides is one of the most variable species in the genus, with forms ranging from pale green to golden-yellow to deep maroon-purple, and its broad, inflated, pouch-like spathe (which gives the species its pitcher-plant-referencing name) can differ dramatically in color even among tubers from the same population. The mottled, snake-skin-patterned false stem supports a single large leaf divided into five to eleven leaflets, unfurling well after the spring flower. Native to mid-elevation Himalayan forests, it is somewhat less cold-hardy than high-alpine Arisaema relatives and benefits from a heavy winter mulch outside its comfortable range. All parts contain calcium oxalate crystals and are toxic and irritating if handled or ingested, so grow it away from pets and children.

planting.note: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in cool, moist, humus-rich, gritty, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in early spring as the ground becomes workable; this high-alpine Himalayan species is one of the most cold-hardy in the genus.

directions: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in cool, moist, humus-rich, gritty, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in early spring as the ground becomes workable; native to high-alpine meadows and forest margins of the Himalayas up to 13,000 feet, Arisaema jacquemontii is one of the most cold-hardy species in the genus, tolerating harsher winters than most of its Himalayan relatives. It produces a slender green spathe boldly striped with white, tapering into a long, thin, upright tail, above a single leaf divided into three to five narrow leaflets on a slim, mottled stem. Its compact size and exceptional hardiness make it a good choice for northern woodland or rock gardens alongside other high-elevation shade plants. Like other jack-in-the-pulpits, the tuber and berries contain irritating calcium oxalate crystals and are toxic if eaten, so site it away from pets and children.

planting.note: Plant the tuber 3-4 inches deep in moist, rich, fast-draining soil in partial to full shade after all danger of frost, in a warm, humid site; move potted specimens under cover for winter outside frost-free zones.

directions: Plant the tuber 3-4 inches deep in moist, rich, fast-draining soil in partial to full shade after all danger of frost, in a warm, humid spot; native to the forests of Java, Amorphophallus muelleri sends up a single, tall, strikingly mottled gray-green and cream petiole resembling a slender tree trunk, topped by one enormous, deeply divided, umbrella-shaped leaf that can span several feet across. Like its relative Amorphophallus bulbifer, mature plants readily produce small aerial bulbils where the leaflets branch, allowing the species to self-propagate freely in a warm, sheltered spot. The brief spring inflorescence, produced by the tuber before leafing out, carries a strong carrion odor for about a day to attract fly pollinators. It is a tender tropical aroid best grown in a large container in temperate climates and moved under cover for winter; all parts contain calcium oxalate crystals and are toxic and irritating if ingested.

planting.note: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; 'Marmoratum' is the named clone most commonly sold for its consistently strong silver-white leaf marbling.

directions: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; 'Marmoratum' is the classic, most widely offered clone of Italian arum, selected and propagated for its consistently bold, silvery-white marbling along the veins of its glossy, arrow-shaped leaves, which is more pronounced and reliable than on seed-grown straight species plants. Foliage emerges in fall and remains an eye-catching feature through the coldest months when most other shade perennials are dormant, dying back by early summer just as a bare flower stalk sets a dense spike of bright orange-red berries. It naturalizes gradually by offsets in the deep, undisturbed shade of mature trees, providing rare off-season winter interest in a woodland garden. All parts of the plant, especially the berries, contain calcium oxalate crystals and are toxic if ingested, so keep it away from pets and children despite its ornamental fruit display.
